title: Moving data, and the instruction that does not move anything
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read any x86-64 memory operand, tell mov and lea apart on sight, and recognise lea being used as arithmetic.

blocks.text: Most instructions in a disassembly are mov. Learning to read its operand forms covers most of what a program does with data, and it also sets up the one instruction that looks like mov, uses the same syntax, and means something entirely different.

blocks.caption: Every memory operand, in one shape
lines: Every memory operand on x86-64 has the same shape:
[ base + index*scale + displacement ]
base          any register
index         any register except rsp
scale         1, 2, 4 or 8 -- nothing else
displacement  a constant
Any part may be omitted. All of these are one instruction:
mov eax, dword ptr [rdi]                 ; *p
mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + 4]             ; p->second_int_field
mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + 4*rsi]         ; a[i]  for int a[]
mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + rsi + 12]      ; base + offset + constant
/* The scale values 1, 2, 4 and 8 are exactly the sizes of char, short,
int and long or pointer. The addressing mode was designed around
array indexing, which is why a[i] costs no extra instruction. */

blocks.title: dword ptr and its relatives
blocks.text: A memory operand has no size of its own, so when the size cannot be inferred from a register the assembler is told explicitly: byte ptr for 1, word ptr for 2, dword ptr for 4, qword ptr for 8. The names are historical — a 'word' was sixteen bits on the 8086 and the term never updated — so read dword as four bytes and qword as eight, and do not try to make the names mean anything.
lea: compute the address, do not go there

lea stands for load effective address. It takes exactly the same bracketed operand as mov, computes the address that operand describes, and puts that address in the destination. It never touches memory. Because the address computation is a multiply-and-add unit sitting right there, compilers use it constantly for arithmetic that has nothing to do with addresses.

blocks.caption: Real compiler output
lines: long times5(long x)  { return x * 5;  }
lea  rax, [rdi + 4*rdi]        ; x + 4x = 5x, one instruction, no multiply
long times12(long x) { return x * 12; }
shl  rdi, 2                    ; x *= 4
lea  rax, [rdi + 2*rdi]        ; 4x + 8x = 12x
int addconst(int x)  { return x + 7;  }
lea  eax, [rdi + 7]            ; used purely as an add that writes elsewhere
int idx(int *a, long i) { return a[i]; }
mov  eax, dword ptr [rdi + 4*rsi]     ; mov: the brackets mean FETCH
/* lea computes the address and stops. mov with the same brackets goes and
gets what is there. Same syntax, opposite meaning -- the single most
common confusion when learning to read x86-64. */

blocks.title: How to tell what a lea is for
blocks.text: If the result is later dereferenced, it was an address. If it is added, compared or returned as a number, it was arithmetic. lea rax, [rdi + 4*rdi] cannot be an address computation at all — no array has a stride of five times its own base — so it is a multiplication by 5. Reading the intent from the use rather than the instruction is the habit this whole course is training.
Why compilers like it so much

rows: Write its result to a different register, leaving both inputs intact
add destroys one of its inputs
Combine three terms at once: base, scaled index and a constant
Multiply by 2, 3, 4, 5, 8 or 9 via the scale plus the base
imul is a separate, slower instruction
Do all of it without touching the flags
add sets flags, which may destroy a pending comparison

blocks.text: The last row is the subtle one and it matters when reading. A compiler that has already compared two values and not yet branched cannot insert an add without losing the comparison result. lea lets it compute in the gap. When you see lea where add would have done, this is often why.

blocks.caption: Three conversions, and one that is free
lines: long widen(int x)                  { return x; }   /* signed */
movsxd rax, edi                ; sign-extend 32 to 64
unsigned long widenu(unsigned x)   { return x; }   /* unsigned */
mov    eax, edi                ; that is the WHOLE function
unsigned char lowbyte(unsigned x)  { return (unsigned char)x; }
movzx  eax, dil                ; zero-extend 8 to 32
/* Zero-extending from 32 to 64 bits needs no instruction at all, because
writing eax already clears the top half -- the rule from the previous
lesson, paying for itself. Sign-extension needs a real instruction
because the fill bits depend on the value. */

blocks.text: movsx and movzx are move-with-sign-extend and move-with-zero-extend. The pair widen and widenu above is the clearest possible demonstration of why the register rule from the previous lesson matters in practice: two functions that look identical in C compile to a real instruction and to nothing at all, purely because of what a 32-bit write does to the upper half.

blocks.title: A missing instruction is information
blocks.text: When you are reading disassembly and an expected conversion is absent, that is not the compiler forgetting. It means the conversion was free given what the previous instruction already guaranteed. Learning which operations leave guarantees behind — a 32-bit write zeroing the top, a comparison leaving flags set — is what makes short compiled sequences readable instead of mysterious.

blocks.caption: Read this before continuing
lines: shl  rsi, 4
mov  eax, dword ptr [rdi + rsi + 12]
Step 1: rsi *= 16
Step 2: load 4 bytes from rdi + rsi + 12
Combined: rdi + 16*i + 12, reading 4 bytes.
16 bytes per element and 12 bytes into it: an array of 4-int structures,
reading the fourth int of element i.
/* The C it came from was: return a[i*4 + 3]; with a of type int*.
Same arithmetic, different way of saying it. */

blocks.title: Read and predict
steps: Compile a function returning a[i] for int, long and char arrays, and compare the scales
Predict the scale for each before looking
Write x*3, x*5, x*7, x*9 and x*10 and see which become a single lea
Explain why 7 needs more work than 5 or 9
Write a function returning a pointer to an array element and one returning the element
Confirm one uses lea and the other mov, with identical bracketed operands
Compile the signed and unsigned widening functions and confirm one is empty
Find a lea in a larger program and decide from its use whether it is an address or arithmetic
blocks.expected: Scales of 4, 8 and 1 matching the element sizes, single-lea multiplications for 3, 5 and 9, and more work for 7 and 10. The reason is that lea can form base + scale*base for scale 1, 2, 4 and 8, giving multipliers 2, 3, 5 and 9 directly — and 7 is not among them. That single observation explains a large fraction of the odd-looking arithmetic in optimised code.

cheatsheet: Every memory operand is [ base + index*scale + displacement ], scale in 1, 2, 4, 8
byte ptr, word ptr, dword ptr, qword ptr mean 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes
'word' means sixteen bits for historical reasons; do not read the names literally
mov with brackets fetches; lea with the same brackets computes the address only
lea rax, [rdi + 4*rdi] is x*5, not an address
lea can write elsewhere, combine three terms, and does not touch the flags
Multipliers 2, 3, 5 and 9 come free from lea; 7 does not
movsxd sign-extends 32 to 64; unsigned widening needs no instruction at all
A missing conversion means it was already guaranteed by the previous instruction

checkpoint.explanation: Lea computes the address expression without accessing memory. No array has a stride of four times its own base address, so this cannot be an address computation. It is a multiplication by five in one instruction.

checkpoint.prompt: You see mov eax, dword ptr [rdi + 4*rsi]. What is this in C?

choices.B: a[i] where a is an int* in rdi and i is in rsi

checkpoint.explanation: Scale 4 is the size of an int. The scale gives the element size. mov with brackets fetches, so this reads the element rather than computing its address.

checkpoint.prompt: unsigned long widenu(unsigned x) { return x; } compiles to a single mov eax, edi. Why is no conversion instruction needed?

choices.A: A 32-bit write already zeroes the upper 32 bits
choices.B: The compiler omitted it by mistake
choices.C: unsigned and unsigned long are the same size
choices.D: The conversion happens at the call site

checkpoint.explanation: Is exactly what zero-extension means. The register rule pays for itself. The signed version needs movsxd because the fill bits depend on the value's sign.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a compiler sometimes use lea where add would work?

choices.D: lea writes to a different register, can combine three terms, and does not disturb the flags

checkpoint.explanation: Which matters when a comparison result is still needed. The flags point is the subtle one: inserting an add between a comparison and its branch would destroy the comparison. lea computes in that gap safely.
